summary: This Level 3 unit covers choosing, using, checking and looking after the hand tools of the welding and fabrication trade, and leading a small team that uses them. You will plan hand-tool work from a drawing; mark out, saw, file, chisel, cut threads, rivet and tighten bolts to a set torque; take the extra precautions needed near flammable vapour, live equipment and at height; and run a tool inspection and control system with proper records.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you learnt to use hand tools safely under supervision. At Level 3 you are expected to **plan** hand-tool work, choose the best tool and method for each step, do the calculations (tapping drills, torque, leverage, blade pitch), **lead and check** a small team, and keep the team's tools safe, in good order and accounted for.

Hand tools are used on every job, even in shops full of power tools: marking out, filing a fit, cutting a thread, tightening a bolt to a set torque, cleaning a weld. Many workshop injuries come from simple hand tools that are misused or badly kept: a mushroomed chisel head, a slipping spanner, a file with no handle, a snapped tap.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training providers, and welders and fabricators who lead small teams in a workshop or on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan hand-tool work
Read the drawing, break the job into steps, choose the tools for each step, check they are fit for use, and share out the work.
Work safely and keep others safe
Use each tool the right way, wear the right PPE, prevent strain injuries, and take the extra precautions near flammable vapour, live equipment and at height.
Mark out and hold the work
Mark accurately with scriber, square, rule and punches; hold work firmly in vices and clamps without damaging it.
Cut and shape by hand
Choose and use hacksaw blades, snips, chisels, punches and files to cut and shape metal to the drawing.
Cut and check threads
Choose tapping drills, cut internal and external threads, identify unknown threads, and remove broken fasteners.
Assemble and tighten
Choose the right spanner or socket, fit blind and solid rivets, and tighten bolts to a set torque.
Inspect and maintain tools
Check tools before and after use, recondition those that can be repaired safely, and take the rest out of use.
Control tools and keep records
Run a tool register, shadow board and sign-out system, tag faulty tools, and report on tool condition.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, special hazards, threading, torque, spanners, chisels, hammers, files, saws, snips, riveting, weld-cleaning tools and tool control.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact names (for example tap wrench, prick punch, A/F, set, single cut) and essays in full sentences, with the working shown for torque and leverage sums.
**Practical tasks** done as a team: plan, make and inspect a bolted bracket using only hand tools; and inspect and recondition a tool kit, set up a tool control system and give a toolbox talk.

blocks.note: Short answers ask for exact trade names. Learn the key terms in the Revision section, and practise the calculations (tapping drill, torque, mechanical advantage, tooth pitch) until you can do them without looking.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning hand-tool work and leading the team

blocks.p: Good hand-tool work starts before anyone picks up a tool. As the team leader you decide the order of work, the tools and gauges, the checks, and who does what.

flow: Read the drawing and job card: material, sizes, tolerances, threads, finish and quantity
Break the job into steps in a sensible order: mark out, cut, file, drill and tap, deburr, check, assemble, tighten
List the tools, gauges and consumables for each step, with spares (blades, cutting fluid, rivets, a second taper tap)
Check that every tool is fit for use; draw it from the store and sign it out
Do the risk assessment and decide the PPE and controls
Share out the tasks and brief the team: the method, the quality checks and the time allowed
Watch progress and quality; check each person's first part before they make more
Clean, check, count and return the tools; record faults; report on the job

head: Step
Typical hand tools
Check made
rows: Marking out
Scriber, steel rule, engineer's square, combination set, dividers, odd-leg calipers, prick and centre punches, layout dye
Lines measured from a datum edge and checked against the drawing before any cutting
Cutting
Hacksaw with the right blade, snips, cold chisel
Cut on the waste side of the line
Shaping and finishing
Files of the right shape and cut, file card, scraper, deburring tool
Size with rule or vernier caliper; radius with a radius gauge; edges deburred
Threading
Tap set, tap wrench, die and die stock, cutting fluid, thread pitch gauge
Thread tried with a bolt, nut or thread gauge
Assembly
Spanners, sockets, hex keys, torque wrench, rivet gun
Torque applied and recorded; rivets fully set
Weld preparation and cleaning
Chipping hammer, wire brushes, files, scrapers
Weld area clean; separate brushes for stainless steel and aluminium

ul: **Suit the material.** A tool made for soft metal may be ruined on hard steel; a carbon steel brush contaminates stainless steel.
**Suit the size.** The right spanner size (A/F), a blade pitch that suits the section, snips rated for the sheet thickness.
**Choose control over convenience.** A ring spanner rather than an adjustable; a file of the right shape rather than forcing a flat file into a curve.
**Check the access.** Is there room to swing the hammer or turn the wrench? A short tool, a ratchet or an offset handle may be needed.
**Think about the place.** Work near flammable vapour, near live equipment or at height needs special tools and controls (next section).

blocks.note: When you list tools, list the spares too: hacksaw blades, a spare file handle, extra rivets, a second taper tap. A team that stops to fetch a blade loses more time than the planning took.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Give each person a clear task and say what "finished" looks like: the size, the tolerance and the finish.
Rotate the tasks. Nobody should saw or file for hours on end.
Check the first part each person makes before they make the rest.
Explain **why**, not only what: a trainee who knows why a tap is turned back is far less likely to snap it.
Stop unsafe work at once, calmly, and show the right way.
At the end, count the tools back in, check them and record any faults before the team leaves.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican workshops have both metric and inch (imperial) fasteners, because much plant, machinery and many vehicles come from the USA. When you work on existing equipment, put both kinds of spanner and both thread gauges on the tool list, and never "make do" with the nearest size.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk, often 5 to 10 minutes, at the start of a job or shift. Keep it to one topic (for example "chisels and punches"), show a real tool, good and faulty, let people ask questions, and record who attended.

Hand tools cause cuts, crushed fingers, eye injuries from flying chips, and strain injuries from repeated work. Most of these come from three things: **the wrong tool, a damaged tool, or a tool used the wrong way.**

head: Rule
Why
rows: Use each tool only for its own job
A screwdriver used as a chisel, or a file used as a lever, can snap and send pieces flying.
Check every tool before use; never use a damaged one
Loose heads fly off; mushroomed heads throw chips; cracked handles break under load.
Pull spanners towards you and stand balanced
If the spanner slips, your knuckles and body do not follow it into the work.
Never lengthen a spanner with a pipe or strike it with a hammer (unless it is a striking spanner made for this)
The overload can break the spanner or the bolt, and you fall or hit the work.
Fit a handle to every file
The pointed tang can drive into your palm or wrist.
Cut away from your body; keep your other hand behind the cutting edge
A slip then goes into the air, not into you.
Clamp the work
Both hands are free to control the tool, and the work cannot spin or fall.
Carry sharp tools pointing down, or in a tool bag
Not in your pockets, where they cut you or others.
Never strike two hardened faces together (hammer on hammer, hammer on a file)
Hardened steel can chip and throw splinters like shrapnel.

ul: **Safety glasses** with side shields at all times; a **face shield** as well when chipping or grinding.

**Gloves** when handling sharp-edged sheet, rough castings or hot metal (cut-resistant gloves for sheet). But **no gloves near rotating machines** such as the pillar drill, where a glove can be caught and pull your hand in.
**Safety boots**: dropped steel, vices and heavy tools crush toes.
**Hearing protection** for long spells of hammering or chipping.

blocks.p: Sawing, filing and tapping for hours can cause **strain injuries**: pain, swelling and numbness in the hands, wrists and forearms, and back pain from bending over a low bench. They build up slowly and can last for years.

ul: Keep tools sharp: a blunt file or blade needs much more force.
Set the vice at about **elbow height**, so the wrist stays straight and the back upright. Use a platform or another bench for shorter or taller people.
Clamp the work, so nobody is gripping it as well as the tool.
Grip firmly but not tightly; use handles that fit the hand.
Rotate tasks and take short breaks; stretch the hands and shoulders.
Report pain early: it is easier to treat.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, sweaty hands slip on tool handles, and tired workers grip harder and make mistakes. Keep a cloth to dry your hands, drink water often, and plan the heaviest hand work for the cooler part of the day where you can.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Place
The danger
Controls
rows: Flammable vapour or dust (fuel tanks, paint stores, gas plant)
A spark from steel striking steel or concrete can ignite the vapour
Work permit and gas test before and during the work
Ventilation
**Non-sparking tools**, usually copper-beryllium or aluminium-bronze
Non-sparking tools reduce the risk; they do not remove it, so the permit and gas testing are still needed
Near electrical equipment
Shock or arc flash if a tool touches a live part
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead, with a tester checked before and after use
Insulated tools (rated 1000 V and marked with the double-triangle symbol) are a back-up only, never a reason to work live
Check the insulation for cuts and cracks before use
At height (platforms, scaffolds, roofs, ladders)
Dropped tools injure people below; carrying tools makes climbing unsafe
Tool lanyards, tool bags or holsters
Haul tools up in a closed bag or bucket on a rope instead of carrying them up a ladder
Barricade and sign the area below
Toe boards on platforms
Inside tanks and confined spaces
Poor air; little room; a tool left inside can wreck a pump or valve later
Confined-space permit
Count tools in and out
Short tools and good lighting
Near moving machinery
A tool caught by a moving part is thrown out, or drags your hand in
Isolate the machine first
Never clear swarf from a running machine with a tool or your hand

blocks.note: Non-sparking tools are much softer than steel tools. They wear, chip and mushroom faster, so check them more often. Copper-beryllium tools give off **toxic dust** when they are ground or dressed: never regrind them on the workshop grinder. Tag them and send them to a supplier who can recondition them safely.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Accurate work starts with accurate marking. Every later step follows the lines you scribe, so a mistake here is copied into the finished part.

head: Tool
Use
Points to know
rows: Scriber
Scratches a fine line on metal
Keep the point sharp; lean it so the point runs tight against the edge of the rule
Layout dye (marking blue)
A thin coat that makes scribed lines easy to see
Clean off oil first and let it dry
Steel rule and tape
Measuring, and guiding the scriber
Measure from a clean datum edge; a worn rule end gives a false reading
Engineer's square
Marking and checking lines at 90° to an edge
Hold the stock firmly against a straight datum edge
Combination set
Square head (90° and 45°), centre head (finds the centre of a bar) and protractor head (angles)
Check it against a known square from time to time
Dividers
Scribing arcs and circles; stepping off equal distances
Set them from the rule; put one leg in a prick-punch mark
Odd-leg (jenny) calipers
Scribing lines parallel to an edge; finding the centre of a bar
The bent leg runs along the edge
Prick punch (point about 30°)
Light, accurate marks along a scribed line, or to locate a divider leg
A light tap only
Centre punch (point about 90°)
Enlarges a prick-punch mark so a drill starts in the right place
Never on a hardened surface
Soapstone and paint markers
Rough marking on hot or rough steel; identifying parts
Not accurate enough for fine work

blocks.note: Mark every measurement from one datum edge or centre line, not from one feature to the next. Chained measurements add their errors together; measurements from a datum do not.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Device
Best for
Points to know
rows: Engineer's bench vice
Holding parts for sawing, filing, chiselling and tapping
Hold the work low in the jaws, close to the cut
Use soft jaws (aluminium, copper or fibre) to protect finished faces
Never hammer the handle or lengthen it with a pipe
Vee jaws or vee blocks
Round bar and tube
The bar sits in the vee, so it cannot roll and is not marked flat
G-clamp (C-clamp)
Holding work to a bench, or parts together
Keep the swivel pad flat on the work; do not tighten it with a bar
F-clamp (sash clamp)
Quick clamping with a long reach
Lighter grip than a G-clamp
Locking (self-grip) welding clamps
Holding plates tight for tacking; locked and released with one hand
Set the adjusting screw first, then lock; keep the jaws out of the spatter
Toggle clamps
Jigs where the same part is held again and again
A worn toggle lets parts move: check it
Magnetic squares and clamps
Holding steel at angles for tacking
Can cause arc blow when welding; no use on stainless steel or aluminium
Hand vice
Small parts that are too small to hold safely in your fingers
Never hold small work by hand when drilling or filing

blocks.note: Do not use the vice body as an anvil unless it has an anvil face: the cast body can crack. Do not open the jaws so far that the moving jaw drops out onto your foot.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A hacksaw blade cuts on the **forward (push) stroke**, so fit it with the teeth pointing away from the handle, and tension it firmly with the wing nut. The teeth are bent a little to the left and right (the **set**), so the cut (the **kerf**) is wider than the blade and the blade does not jam.
Blade pitch is given in **TPI** (teeth per inch; 1 inch = 25.4 mm). **Tooth pitch in mm = 25.4 ÷ TPI.**

head: Blade
Tooth pitch
Typical use
rows: 14 TPI
about 1.8 mm
Soft metals and large solid sections
18 TPI
about 1.4 mm
General work: solid mild steel bar and thick flat
24 TPI
about 1.1 mm
Angle, flat bar and tube about 3–6 mm thick
32 TPI
about 0.8 mm
Thin-walled tube, conduit and sheet under about 3 mm

blocks.p: The main rule: **at least three teeth should be in the cut at all times.** With too few teeth, each tooth catches on the thin edge and is stripped off. With too many (a fine blade on a thick solid bar), the gaps between the teeth fill with chips and the blade stops cutting and overheats.

flow: Choose the blade for the thinnest part to be cut; fit it teeth forward and tension it
Clamp the work low in the vice, with the cut close to the jaws
File a small nick on the waste side of the line to start the cut
Start with light strokes at a low angle, guiding the blade with your thumb well clear
Use the whole length of the blade at a steady pace (about 40–60 strokes a minute); press on the forward stroke and ease off on the return
Turn thin sections so you always cut at a slant through the wall, never straight down onto a thin edge
Slow down at the end and support the off-cut so it does not drop or tear

ul: A new blade will jam in a cut started with an old one, because the worn blade cut a narrower kerf. Turn the work over and start a new cut.
Blades are carbon steel (cheap, snap easily), high-speed steel, or **bi-metal** (high-speed teeth on a flexible back: tough and long-lasting, the usual choice).
A junior hacksaw takes short, fine blades for small work.

blocks.note: Fast, short strokes heat the teeth and blunt them quickly. Steady strokes that use the whole blade cut faster in the end.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Use
rows: Straight snips (tin snips)
Straight cuts and gentle curves in sheet
Aviation (compound) snips: straight, left-cut and right-cut
A compound action gives more cutting force. Left-cut snips cut curves to the left, right-cut snips curves to the right. Handles are often colour-coded, but check the maker's marking.
Bench (lever) shears
Heavier sheet and small flat bar, within the rated capacity
Hand nibbler
Cut-outs inside a sheet, with very little distortion

ul: Every pair of snips has a **maximum thickness**, often about 1.2 mm for mild steel and noticeably less for stainless steel, which is harder. Over that rating the blades chip, the pivot spreads and the cut edge is torn.
To cut a hole in the middle of a sheet, drill or punch a starting hole in the waste, then cut out to the line.
Cut edges are razor sharp: wear gloves, and deburr the edges afterwards with a file or deburring tool.

head: Chisel
Use
rows: Flat cold chisel
Cutting sheet, bar and rivet heads; chipping
Cross-cut (cape) chisel
Cutting narrow grooves and keyways
Half-round chisel
Cutting curved grooves
Diamond-point chisel
Cutting V-grooves and cleaning out sharp corners

blocks.p: A cold chisel for mild steel is usually ground to a point angle of about **60°**, with the edge slightly curved so its corners do not dig in. Softer metals take a slightly smaller angle and hard or brittle metals a larger one: follow your instructor.

ul: Strike with a **club (lump) hammer** for heavy cutting, or a ball pein hammer for light work. Watch the cutting edge, not the head.
Hold the chisel loosely, or use a chisel holder or hand guard, so a missed blow does not land on your hand.
Wear safety glasses, and put up a screen so chips do not hit other people.
Dress (grind off) a mushroomed head before it gets bad (see the last section).

head: Punch
Use
rows: Pin punch (parallel)
Driving pins out of holes
Drift (taper punch)
Starting pins; lining up holes
Hollow (wad) punch
Cutting round holes in gaskets, rubber and leather, struck on end-grain wood or a soft block
Letter and number punches
Marking parts and tools (never on a hardened working face)

head: Hammer
Use
rows: Ball pein (engineer's) hammer
General work; the rounded pein is for peening and forming rivet heads
Cross pein and straight pein
Spreading and shaping metal in one direction
Club (lump) hammer
Heavy blows on chisels, punches and striking spanners
Sledgehammer
Very heavy blows, swung with both hands, with everyone well clear
Soft-faced and dead-blow hammers
Rubber, plastic, copper or rawhide faces do not mark finished work; a dead-blow head is filled with shot so it does not bounce back
Chipping hammer
Removing slag from welds

ul: Hold the hammer near the end of the handle and let its weight do the work.
The hammer face should be a little larger than the head of the tool you strike, and should hit it squarely.
Check that the head is tight and the face is not chipped before use.

blocks.p: The parts of a file are the **tang** (which goes into the handle), the heel, the face, the edges (one may be a **safe edge** with no teeth) and the point. Files are described by length, shape and cut.

head: Feature
Types
Use
rows: Cut (pattern of teeth)
Single cut: one set of parallel rows
Double cut: two sets crossing
Rasp: separate raised teeth
Single: finishing, soft metals, sharpening
Double: faster general removal
Rasp: wood and plastics
Grade (coarseness)
Rough, bastard, second cut, smooth, dead smooth
Coarse grades remove metal fast; smooth grades give the finish
Shape
Flat, hand (one safe edge), half-round, round, square, three-square (triangular), knife, needle files
Half-round: concave (inside) curves
Round: small holes and tight curves
Square: slots and square holes
Three-square: corners under 90°
Hand file: filing up to a shoulder without marking it

ul: **Cross filing**: across the work, changing direction now and then to show the high spots. For removing metal quickly.
**Draw filing**: the file held crosswise in both hands and pushed and pulled along the length of the work. For a fine, flat finish on a long edge.
Press on the forward stroke only and ease off on the return, or the teeth are dulled.
Keep the file level; rock it only when filing a convex curve.
Clean the teeth with a **file card**. Bits of metal stuck in the teeth (**pinning**) scratch the work. Rubbing chalk into the teeth helps stop soft metals such as aluminium clogging them.
Never oil a file, and never use one as a lever or a hammer: files are hard and brittle and can shatter.
Use new files on brass and other soft metals first, and older ones on steel: a file dulled by steel will not bite brass.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Major diameter
The largest diameter of the thread: the 10 mm in M10
Pitch
The distance from one thread crest to the next. In M10 × 1.5 the pitch is 1.5 mm.
Coarse and fine series
M10 coarse has a 1.5 mm pitch; M10 fine is 1.25 mm or 1.0 mm. The pitch is often left off coarse threads: M10 means M10 × 1.5.
Minor diameter
The diameter at the root of the thread
Inch (imperial) threads
UNC and UNF (from the USA), BSW and BSF (older British), and pipe threads (BSP, NPT); sized in inches, with the pitch given in threads per inch
Thread pitch (screw pitch) gauge
A set of blades with teeth of known pitch, held against a thread to identify it

blocks.p: **To identify an unknown thread:** measure the major diameter with a vernier caliper, find the pitch with a thread pitch gauge (try metric and inch blades), then look it up in a thread table.

For metric coarse threads the **tapping drill is about the major diameter minus the pitch**. That leaves enough metal for a strong thread (about 75–80% of full depth) without making the tap too hard to turn. Always check a tapping-drill chart.

head: Thread
Pitch
Tapping drill
rows: M6
1.0 mm
5.0 mm
M8
6.8 mm
1.5 mm
8.5 mm
2.0 mm
2.5 mm

blocks.note: For M12: 12 − 1.75 = 10.25 mm, so the chart gives the nearest standard drill, 10.2 mm. A drill that is too small makes the tap bind and snap; one that is too large leaves a shallow, weak thread that strips.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Tap
Lead (tapered start)
Use
rows: Taper (first) tap
Long taper, about 8–10 threads
Starts the thread square and cuts most of it; in a through hole it can cut the full thread on its own
Second (intermediate) tap
Shorter taper, about 3–5 threads
Follows the taper tap and carries the full thread further down
Plug (bottoming) tap
Almost no taper, 1–2 threads
Cuts full thread close to the bottom of a blind hole

flow: Mark, centre punch and drill the tapping hole; in a blind hole, drill deeper than the thread needed
Chamfer the top of the hole so the tap starts easily
Clamp the work with the hole upright
Fit the taper tap in a tap wrench of the right size and start it square; check with a small square from two sides, 90° apart
Apply cutting fluid
Turn forward about half to one turn, then back about a quarter to a half turn to break the chip
In a blind hole, take the tap out often and clear the chips
Follow with the second tap, and the plug tap in a blind hole
Clean out the hole and check the thread with a bolt or a thread plug gauge

ul: **Cutting fluid:** tapping compound or cutting oil for steel; paraffin (kerosene) or the maker's fluid for aluminium. Cast iron and brass are usually tapped dry.
If the tap gets stiff, **stop**. Back it out, clear the chips and start again. Forcing it snaps it.
Use a tap wrench that suits the tap size. A big wrench on a small tap gives so much leverage that you feel nothing before it breaks.

Taps are **hard and brittle**. A broken tap cannot be drilled out with an ordinary drill: it needs a tap extractor (which grips the flutes) or specialist removal by spark erosion. Prevention is everything.

A **die** cuts an external thread on a rod. A split circular (button) die is held in a **die stock**; its adjusting screws open or close it a little, so the first cut can be light and the last cut full size.
The rod should be the major diameter or a little under (for example about 9.8–9.9 mm for M10), and its end **chamfered**, so the die starts square and the first threads are not torn.
Start with the die's chamfered (lead) side on the rod. Keep the die stock square, use cutting fluid, and turn forward and back to break the chip, as with a tap.
Try the thread with a nut or ring gauge. If the nut is tight, adjust the die to cut slightly smaller and run it down again.

flow: Soak the thread with penetrating oil and give it time to work
If any of the stud sticks out, try a stud extractor or locking pliers on it
File or grind the broken end flat and centre punch it exactly in the middle
Drill a pilot hole of the size the extractor chart gives, keeping it central and straight
Tap in a **screw extractor** (reverse spiral) and turn it anticlockwise steadily with a tap wrench
If it will not move, stop: apply heat where it is allowed, or drill the bolt out and re-tap the hole

blocks.note: A screw extractor is hard and brittle. Turn it steadily with a tap wrench, never with a long bar or by hammering. If an extractor snaps in the hole, you are left with a hardened piece that is far harder to remove than the bolt was. A left-hand drill bit sometimes catches and unscrews the broken bolt on its own.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Strong points
Weak points and care
rows: Open-ended spanner
Fits from the side, for example on pipe unions; quick
Grips only two flats; can slip and round off a tight nut
Ring spanner
Grips all six corners; the best spanner for breaking a tight nut loose
Must be lifted off and on over the nut
Combination spanner
A ring at one end and an open end at the other, the same size
As above
Flare-nut (line) spanner
A ring with a slot, so it passes over a pipe and grips most of the faces of a pipe nut
Made for brake, fuel and hydraulic pipe nuts, which are soft and round off easily
Adjustable spanner
Fits many sizes; handy when the right size is not there
The most likely to slip: set it tight and pull so the load is on the fixed jaw
Sockets: 6-point and 12-point
Quick with a ratchet. 6-point grips the flats: best on tight or rusted nuts. 12-point fits in more positions in tight spaces.
12-point rounds off a tight nut more easily; only impact sockets on impact tools
Hex (Allen) keys
Socket-head screws. Long arm in your hand (short end in the screw) for leverage; short arm in your hand for speed.
Replace rounded keys; replace rounded screws
Pipe wrench
Pipe and round bar: its teeth bite harder as the load rises
Never on nuts: the teeth chew the flats
Torque wrench
Final tightening to a set torque
Never for undoing; handle with care
Striking (slogging) spanner
Large nuts on heavy flanges, struck with a club hammer
Only spanners made for striking may be struck

blocks.p: Spanner sizes are marked **A/F (across flats)**: the distance between opposite flats of the nut, for example 19 A/F. Metric and inch sizes are not interchangeable: a 9/16 in spanner (about 14.3 mm) is loose on a 14 mm nut and will round it off.

blocks.note: Pull, don't push. If you have to push, use the flat of your open hand, so your knuckles are not hurt when the nut suddenly gives.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Torque** is a turning force. **Torque = force × distance** from the centre of the nut, with the distance in metres. The unit is the **newton metre (N·m)**.
A **lever** multiplies your effort. **Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm**, where each arm is measured from the pivot (fulcrum).

head: Example
Working
Answer
rows: A 150 N pull on a spanner, 250 mm from the centre of the nut
A bolt needs 90 N·m; the torque wrench grip is 0.45 m from the square drive
200 N at the grip
A pinch bar 1.0 m long rests on a block 0.2 m from the load end
Effort arm 0.8 m ÷ load arm 0.2 m
Mechanical advantage 4: a 100 N push lifts about 400 N (ignoring friction)

blocks.h: Why bolts are tightened to a set torque

blocks.p: Tightening stretches the bolt slightly, like a spring, and that stretch **clamps the joint**. Too little torque and the joint leaks or works loose with vibration. Too much and the bolt stretches for good, the thread strips or a gasket is crushed. Oiled threads give more clamping force at the same torque than dry ones, so tighten them exactly as the specification says (dry or oiled).

flow: Check the calibration label is in date and the wrench is undamaged
Set the torque the specification gives and lock the setting
Run all the nuts down snug with an ordinary spanner
Tighten in a **cross (star) pattern**, in two or three stages (for example a third, two-thirds, then full torque)
Pull smoothly on the handle grip, at right angles to the wrench, and stop at the click: no jerking, and no pulling on past the click
Go round once more at full torque in the same pattern
Record the torque and the wrench number if the job asks for it
Wind the setting back to its lowest value, wipe the wrench clean and put it in its case

ul: Never use a torque wrench to undo nuts, or as a hammer or lever: that damages the mechanism and spoils its accuracy.
Use it inside its range, and preferably not in the bottom fifth of its scale, where it is least accurate.
Have it checked (calibrated) at set intervals, often every 12 months or as the maker says, **and after any drop**. Until then it is out of use.
Winding a click wrench back takes the load off the spring inside. Left wound up, the spring weakens and the wrench reads wrong.

blocks.note: Many torque wrenches and manuals in Jamaica come from the USA and are marked in foot-pounds (ft·lb). 1 ft·lb is about 1.36 N·m, so 60 ft·lb is about 81 N·m. Set the wrench in the units the specification uses, or convert carefully and have someone check it: never guess.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A blind rivet is set from one side only. The **rivet gun** grips the mandrel and pulls it; the mandrel head swells the rivet body on the far side and then snaps off.

head: Rivet diameter
Typical drill (check the maker's chart)
rows: 3.2 mm
3.3 mm
4.0 mm
4.1 mm
4.8 mm
4.9 mm
6.4 mm
6.5 mm

ul: **Grip range** is the total thickness of material a rivet can join; it is printed on the box. Too short and the rivet cannot form; too long and it forms loosely.
Hole too large: the rivet is loose and may pull through. Hole too small: it will not go in.
Deburr the holes on both sides so the sheets sit flat and tight together.
Hold the gun square and pressed firmly against the work; pull until the mandrel snaps; collect the spent mandrels.
Match the rivet metal to the job: aluminium rivets in aluminium, stainless rivets in stainless steel. Mixed metals can corrode each other where it is damp or salty (**galvanic corrosion**).

blocks.note: Near the coast (Kingston Harbour, Portland, the north coast) the salt air speeds up corrosion. Steel or stainless rivets in aluminium sheet make the aluminium around each rivet corrode fast. Use the rivet the specification calls for, with sealant or washers where it says.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A solid rivet passes through both parts, and its tail is formed into a head with a ball pein hammer and a rivet **snap** (shaped die), with a **dolly** holding the first head.
A **rivet set** is struck first to draw the plates tight together over the rivet.
For a round (snap) head, the tail usually sticks out about 1.5 times the rivet diameter; a countersunk head needs less. Follow the drawing.

blocks.h: Hand tools for weld preparation and cleaning

head: Tool
Use
Care
rows: Chipping hammer
Removing slag
Safety glasses or goggles under the helmet; chip away from your face and from other people
Carbon steel wire brushes
Rust, scale and slag on carbon steel
Never on stainless steel or aluminium
Stainless steel wire brushes, marked
Stainless steel, and aluminium: a separate set for each metal
Kept apart and marked with coloured tape
Files and scrapers
Burrs, sharp edges, bevels and root faces; paint near the joint
Separate files for aluminium, which clogs files and picks up steel
Tip cleaners
Clearing the holes in oxy-fuel nozzles
Use the size that fits the hole; push straight in and out without enlarging it
Fillet gauge, bevel protractor, hi-lo (misalignment) gauge
Checking weld sizes, bevel angles and plate or pipe alignment
Kept clean; checked against known sizes
Soapstone, scriber, centre punch
Marking cut lines and weld positions
Soapstone for hot or rough steel

blocks.note: Iron particles from a carbon steel brush, file or disc stick in stainless steel and rust there, leaving brown stains, and they spoil aluminium welds. Keep separate, marked tools for each metal, store them apart, and keep stainless and aluminium work off carbon steel benches.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Tool
Faults to look for
Action
rows: Hammers
Loose or cracked head; split handle; chipped or mushroomed face
Re-handle and wedge; scrap a hammer with a chipped face
Chisels and punches
Mushroomed head; blunt or chipped edge; bent or cracked
Dress the head; regrind the edge; scrap if cracked
Screwdrivers
Rounded or twisted tip; cracked handle; bent shaft
Regrind a flat tip square, or replace; replace cross-point (Phillips) screwdrivers
Spanners and sockets
Spread or cracked jaws; rounded rings
Scrap: never squeeze jaws back together
Adjustable spanners and pipe wrenches
Worn worm or teeth; play in the jaw
Clean and oil; replace when worn
Files
Clogged teeth; worn smooth; no handle; cracked
File card; fit a handle; scrap when worn out
Hacksaws and snips
Bent frame; nicked or blunt blade; loose pivot
Replace the blade; adjust the pivot; send snips for sharpening
Taps and dies
Chipped or worn teeth
Replace: worn taps cut rough, oversize threads
Torque wrench
Out of calibration date; dropped; damaged scale
Out of use until checked
Insulated tools
Cut, cracked or worn insulation
Scrap: never tape over it
Vices and clamps
Bent screws; cracked bodies; worn jaws
Repair or scrap

ul: **Chisel and punch heads:** grind off the mushroom and leave a smooth chamfer (bevel) around the struck end, so no loose pieces can fly off.

**Cold chisel edges:** grind to the right angle with a slight curve. Use light pressure, keep the tool moving across the wheel, and **dip it in water often**. If the edge turns straw then blue, it has been overheated and has lost its hardness: grind back past the coloured part, or have it re-hardened and tempered.
**Flat screwdriver tips:** grind or file the faces flat and parallel and the end square, keeping the tip cool; replace the screwdriver if the tip is too short or cracked.

**Hammer handles:** take off the old handle, fit a sound new one that fills the eye of the head, and drive a **wedge** across the top of the handle to spread it and lock the head. Soaking a loose wooden handle in water swells it only for a while; it then shrinks back looser. Replace cracked fibreglass or steel handles.
**Files:** clean with a file card; pick out stubborn pins with a soft metal pick.
**All steel tools:** wipe clean, oil lightly against rust, and store dry.

blocks.note: Grind only with the guards in place, the tool rest set close to the wheel (about 3 mm or less), safety glasses and a face shield. Grind on the face of the wheel, never the side unless it is made for that. At the Centre, bench grinding is done only under the instructor's direct supervision.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Part of the system
What it does
rows: Tool register
Lists every tool with its number, description, location and condition. Number tools by etching or engraving, never by stamping a working face.
Shadow board or foam-cut drawers
An outline for every tool: a gap shows at a glance what is out
Sign-out sheet
Name, date, time out and back, and condition on return: you know who has each tool
Inspection colour code
A coloured tape or tag for each month's inspection. A tool without this month's colour is not issued until it has been checked.
DO NOT USE tags and a quarantine box
Faulty tools are tagged with the fault and date, taken out of the kit and recorded
Tool counts
At the end of each day, and before leaving a tank, a machine or work at height, so a lost tool is found before it causes harm
Records of checks and repairs
Show that tools were checked, show which tools fail often, and help plan repairs, replacements and the tool budget (in J$)

blocks.note: A spanner left in a tank, a gearbox or on a roof beam can cause serious damage or injury later. Count the tools in and out, every time.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can plan hand-tool work from a drawing: steps, tools, checks, people and time.
I can brief and lead a small team, rotate tasks and check each person's first part.
I can explain the general rules for safe hand-tool use and the PPE needed.
I can take the right precautions near flammable vapour, near electrical equipment, at height and in confined spaces.
I can explain how to prevent strain injuries in long spells of hand work.
I can mark out accurately from a datum, and hold work securely without damaging it.
I can choose a hacksaw blade by TPI, work out its tooth pitch, and saw thin and thick sections correctly.
I can choose and use snips, chisels, punches, hammers and files for each job.
I can work out a tapping drill, cut internal threads with taps in the right order, and cut external threads with a die.
I can identify an unknown thread and remove a broken bolt safely.
I can choose the right spanner, socket or wrench and use it safely.
I can calculate torque and mechanical advantage, and use and care for a torque wrench.
I can fit blind and solid rivets, choosing the hole size and grip range.
I can choose and keep separate the hand tools for preparing and cleaning carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminium.
I can inspect tools, recondition the ones that can be repaired, and take the rest out of use.
I can set up and run a tool control system and keep its records.

terms: A/F (across flats)
The distance between opposite flats of a nut or bolt head; the size marked on a spanner
Bi-metal blade
A saw blade with high-speed steel teeth on a tough, flexible back
Centre punch
A punch with a point of about 90°, used to locate a drill
Die
A tool that cuts an external thread on a rod; held in a die stock
Draw filing
Filing with the file held crosswise and moved along the length of the work, for a flat, fine finish
Dead-blow hammer
A soft-faced hammer filled with shot, so it does not bounce back
File card
A wire brush for cleaning the teeth of a file
Grip range
The total thickness of material a blind rivet can join
Kerf
The width of the cut made by a saw blade or a cutting process
Mechanical advantage
Effort arm ÷ load arm: how many times a lever multiplies the effort
Mushroomed head
The spread, cracked struck end of a chisel or punch
Non-sparking tools
Tools of copper-beryllium or aluminium-bronze, used where flammable vapour may be present
Pinning
Bits of metal stuck in a file's teeth, which scratch the work
Pitch (thread)
The distance from one thread crest to the next, in mm
Prick punch
A punch with a fine point of about 30° for light marks along a line
Safe edge
An edge of a file with no teeth
Screw extractor
A hardened tool with a reverse spiral, used to remove a broken bolt from a drilled hole
Set (saw teeth)
The teeth bent alternately left and right, so the cut is wider than the blade
Shadow board
A board with an outline for each tool, showing at a glance which are missing
Single cut / double cut
A file with one set of parallel rows of teeth / with two sets crossing
Tap wrench
The handle with a central square socket that holds and turns a hand tap
Tapping drill
The drill used before tapping; for metric coarse threads about the major diameter minus the pitch
Taper, second and plug taps
The three hand taps, used in that order; the plug tap cuts full thread near the bottom of a blind hole
Three-square file
A file with a triangular cross-section
Torque
Turning force: force × distance, in newton metres (N·m)
TPI
Teeth per inch; tooth pitch in mm = 25.4 ÷ TPI

c1.title: Pump-house brackets in Yallahs
c1.text: Kimone, a Level 3 trainee, is leading two newer trainees, Javani and Petagaye, in making six brackets for a pump house in Yallahs, St Thomas. Each bracket is hacksawn from 10 mm mild steel plate, filed to a concave corner of 25 mm radius, and has two M12 coarse threaded through holes, to be cut by hand. Javani has started tapping the first hole with a large tap wrench borrowed from the M20 set.

c2.title: A flange on a generator fuel line in Port Maria
c2.text: Delroy leads a small team replacing a gasket on a flanged diesel line beside the day tank in the generator room of a hospital in Port Maria, St Mary. The work permit requires gas testing, and the team has been issued a set of copper-beryllium (non-sparking) spanners. The eight flange bolts must be tightened to 120 N·m with a click-type torque wrench whose hand grip is 0.5 m from the square drive.

c3.title: The monthly tool check at a training centre in Kingston
c3.text: Shericka is helping her instructor with the monthly tool check at a training centre in Kingston. The centre uses a shadow board, a sign-out sheet and a coloured tape for each month's inspection: this month's colour is green, and last month's was yellow. Among the tools she finds: a cold chisel whose edge has turned dark blue after grinding; a 9/16 in spanner hanging in the metric set next to the 14 mm one; a hammer with a loose wooden handle that someone has left soaking in a bucket of water; and a ball pein hammer that has only yellow tape on it.

c4.title: A stainless kitchen hood in Ocho Rios
c4.text: Rushane's team is making a kitchen extract hood for a hotel in Ocho Rios, St Ann, from 0.9 mm stainless steel sheet on a frame of 1.2 mm stainless angle. The joints are riveted with stainless blind rivets; the rivet boxes in the store are marked with grip ranges of 0.5–3.0 mm and 3.0–5.0 mm. The team's aviation snips are marked as rated for 1.2 mm mild steel and 0.7 mm stainless steel.

c5.title: Handrail bolts on a church tower in Falmouth
c5.text: Oneil and a helper must replace rusted bolts on the steel handrail around the top of a church bell tower in Falmouth, Trelawny, about 15 m up. The only way up is a fixed vertical ladder, and church members walk through the yard below during the day. Several of the old nuts are badly rusted onto their bolts.

questions.q: Which drill should Kimone issue for the M12 holes?
o: 9.5 mm
questions.why: For metric coarse threads the tapping drill is about the major diameter minus the pitch: 12 − 1.75 = 10.25 mm, so the chart gives 10.2 mm. A larger drill leaves a shallow, weak thread; a smaller one makes the tap bind and snap.

questions.q: Why should Kimone stop Javani using the wrench from the M20 set on the M12 tap?
o: The large wrench will make the thread cut oversize
He will not feel the tap binding before it snaps
The thread will come out with the wrong pitch
The wrench will wear away the tap's square end
questions.why: A large wrench gives so much leverage that the tap can be overloaded without the user feeling any resistance. Use a tap wrench that suits the tap, so you feel it tighten and can back off.

questions.q: Despite this, a tap snaps off level with the plate surface. What should the team do?
o: Stop and plan removal with a tap extractor or spark erosion
Drill the broken tap out with a 10.2 mm high-speed drill
Run the second tap in from the top to cut past the piece
Drill a pilot hole in it and turn it out with a screw extractor
questions.why: A tap is hardened and brittle, so an ordinary drill cannot cut it and a screw extractor cannot be fitted into it. It must be gripped by the flutes with a tap extractor, or removed by spark erosion; the team should stop and report it.

questions.q: How should Kimone check the filed 25 mm corner radius?
o: Measure across the curve with a vernier caliper
Check the corner against an engineer's square
Fit a 25 mm radius gauge and look for light
Compare the curve by eye with the drawing
questions.why: A radius gauge has the exact curve cut in it. Held against the work, any gap shows as light, so you can see where to file. Calipers and squares do not check a curve's shape.

questions.q: A team member offers to clean up a burred copper-beryllium spanner on the bench grinder. What should Delroy say?
o: Yes, but wear a face shield and keep it cool
No: file it smooth by hand at the work site
Yes, as long as it is dipped in water often
No: tag it and send it to be reconditioned
questions.why: Grinding or filing copper-beryllium makes toxic dust, so these tools are not dressed in the workshop. A damaged non-sparking tool is tagged, taken out of use and sent to a supplier who can recondition it safely.

questions.q: What steady force must Delroy apply at the grip to reach 120 N·m?
questions.why: Torque = force × distance, so force = torque ÷ distance = 120 ÷ 0.5 = 240 N. The wrench clicks when the set torque is reached, so the force is applied smoothly at the hand grip.

questions.q: In what order should the eight flange bolts be tightened?
o: Round the flange in turn, each one to full torque
Top and bottom first to full torque, then the rest
In a cross (star) pattern, in two or three stages
All to full torque, then each slackened a quarter turn
questions.why: Tightening opposite bolts in stages pulls the flange down evenly onto the gasket. Going round in turn to full torque tilts the flange, so the gasket is crushed on one side and the joint can leak.

questions.q: Halfway through, the torque wrench falls off the flange onto the concrete floor. What should happen?
o: Carry on, as long as it still clicks
Use it only for the bolts already started
Add about 10% to the setting to be safe
Take it out of use until it is checked
questions.why: A drop can upset the mechanism, so the wrench may click at the wrong torque without any sign. It is taken out of use and checked before the bolts are finally tightened and recorded.

questions.q: What does the dark blue colour on the chisel's cutting edge tell Shericka?
o: The edge was overheated and has lost its hardness
It is only surface colour, which a polish will remove
The edge has been hardened further and will last longer
The chisel has cracked inside and must be scrapped
questions.why: Steel that turns straw then blue on the grinder has been heated enough to soften it, so the edge will blunt quickly. Grind back past the coloured part, keeping it cool, or have it re-hardened and tempered.

questions.q: What should Shericka recommend for the hammer with the loose wooden handle?
o: Leave it in the water overnight so the handle swells tight
Fit a new handle that fills the head, then wedge it
Wrap insulating tape round the handle below the head
Drive a nail through the side of the head into the handle
questions.why: Soaking swells the handle only for a while; it then dries and shrinks looser than before. A sound new handle that fills the eye, locked with a wedge across the top, holds the head safely.

questions.q: Why is the 9/16 in spanner a problem in the metric set?
o: It is slightly too big and will round off the nut
It is slightly too small to fit over a 14 mm nut
It is the same size, so either may be used on 14 mm
It grips tighter, so it is the better one for 14 mm
questions.why: 9/16 in is about 14.3 mm, so on a 14 mm nut it sits loose, grips the corners and rounds them off. Metric and inch spanners are kept in their own sets and used only on their own fasteners.

questions.q: What should happen to the ball pein hammer with only yellow tape?
o: Issue it, as last month's check is still good enough
Throw it away, as it has missed an inspection
Put green tape on it now to bring it up to date
Hold it back until it is checked and taped green
questions.why: The colour code shows which tools passed this month's check. A tool with last month's colour has not been checked this month, so it is held back, inspected, and only then given the current colour.

questions.q: Each joint is one sheet of 0.9 mm on 1.2 mm angle. Which rivets should Rushane use?
o: 0.5–3.0 mm grip, as the joint is 2.1 mm thick
3.0–5.0 mm grip, so there is plenty of length
0.5–3.0 mm grip, as the sheet is under 1 mm
Either box, since a blind rivet adjusts itself
questions.why: The grip range must include the total thickness being joined: 0.9 + 1.2 = 2.1 mm, which falls in the 0.5–3.0 mm range. A rivet that is too long forms loosely and does not clamp the joint tight.

questions.q: Can the team cut the 0.9 mm stainless sheet with their aviation snips?
o: Yes: 0.9 mm is under the 1.2 mm on the snips
Yes, as long as they oil the blades well before cutting
No: aviation snips cannot cut stainless at all
No: it is above the stainless rating, so use shears
questions.why: Stainless steel is harder than mild steel, so snips carry a lower rating for it, here 0.7 mm. Cutting 0.9 mm would chip the blades and spread the pivot; use bench shears or a nibbler rated for the job.

questions.q: What should be done to the drilled rivet holes before the rivets go in?
o: Paint them with primer to seal the edges
Deburr both sides so the sheets sit tight
Open them out 0.5 mm so rivets fit easily
Leave them, as the rivet flattens the burrs
questions.why: Burrs hold the sheets apart, so the rivet cannot pull them tight and the joint stays loose. Deburr both sides; an oversize hole would let the rivet sit loose or pull through.

questions.q: How should Oneil get his tools to the top of the tower?
o: Carry them up in his pockets and a belt pouch
Pass them up one at a time to the helper above him
Climb up first, then haul them up in a closed bag
Throw the light ones up to the helper on top
questions.why: Climbing a fixed ladder needs both hands free. Hauling the tools up in a closed bag on a rope, with the area below cleared, keeps hands free and stops tools falling on people below.

questions.q: A rusted nut will not move. What is the best first step?
o: Soak it with penetrating oil, wait, then use a ring spanner
Slide a length of pipe over the spanner for more leverage
Use a pipe wrench, because its teeth bite harder on rusty nuts
Strike the open-ended spanner with a club hammer
questions.why: Penetrating oil needs time to work into the rust, and a ring spanner grips all six corners. Extra leverage, hammering an ordinary spanner or a pipe wrench can break the bolt or round the nut, and at height a slip can mean a fall.

questions.q: Kirk uses a 1.2 m pinch bar to raise the corner of a heavy machine base. The bar rests on a block 150 mm from the lifted end. About how many times does the bar multiply his effort?
o: 8 times
7 times
6 times
1.25 times
questions.why: Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. The load arm is 150 mm and the effort arm is 1200 − 150 = 1050 mm, so 1050 ÷ 150 = 7 (ignoring friction).

questions.q: A trainee drives a stuck club hammer out of a bench hole by striking its face with a ball pein hammer. What is the main danger?
o: The ball pein hammer's handle may split along its length
The club hammer may be driven in even tighter
Hardened faces can chip and throw sharp splinters
The noise is loud enough to damage his hearing
questions.why: Hammer faces are hardened. When two hardened faces strike each other, chips can fly off at high speed like shrapnel. Use a soft drift or a soft-faced hammer instead.

questions.q: Why should a screw extractor be turned with a tap wrench, never with a long bar?
o: A bar would turn the extractor in the wrong direction
The extractor is soft and would bend under a long bar
If it snaps, a hardened piece is left in the hole
A tap wrench grips the extractor's spiral more tightly
questions.why: Extractors are hardened and brittle. Too much leverage snaps them, leaving a piece that is much harder to remove than the original bolt. Turn steadily with a tap wrench and stop if it will not move.
